packs.title: Coast, Canals & Culture
packs.promise: Find small adventures between the ocean, cultural collections and a grounded cockpit.

q.s: Let three short rounds change what you notice.
st: Find a comfortable seat or standing place beside the white wave wall, clear of the walking route.
Spend one short round attending to a repeating movement: small waves, palm fronds or changing patches of light. Use sight, sound or both.
In a second round, notice a variation within that repetition. In a third, return to the whole scene without counting.
Record one thing that repeated and one small change. There is no correct rhythm or required feeling.

q.s: Collect three views of one object.
st: Choose one publicly viewable object with an identifying label, or open the library’s Dogon Ladder 3D model. Read its title and documented place of origin.
Collect a front, side and rear observation. For a physical display, change only your viewing position where permitted; never handle it. For the model, rotate the view.
Before the third view, predict a detail that might continue around the object. Check whether it does and record the result.
Add the object’s name, the collection’s stated origin and its documented use to your three-view notes. Let the label supply cultural meaning rather than guessing from appearance.

q.s: Give two forms a small invented conversation.
st: Choose one work in an open gallery that holds your attention. Read its title and artist, then choose two visible forms: perhaps a building and a tree, a bright patch and a dark patch, or two objects.
Give each form a different wish based on one visible detail. A leaning line could want to move; a broad block might want to stay.
Write a four-line invented dialogue, alternating between the two forms. Include the two visual details that prompted it.
Read it silently and change one line so the two voices sound different. Keep the work’s actual title and artist beside your fiction.

packs.title: Riverwalk Stories
packs.promise: Turn two downtown afternoons into small experiments, stories and discoveries beside the New River.

q.s: Let one practical priority shape a short walk.
st: From the public path, choose a reachable turning point a few minutes away. Decide whether your priority is a direct route, shade or a place to rest.
Look ahead for two route features that affect that choice. Follow the suitable public path at your own pace, staying out of marina operations.
At your turning point, compare your expectation with the route. Change one part of your return plan if needed.
Record your priority, the two route features and what you would tell a friend before they set out. A very short out-and-back is enough.

q.s: Pack three kinds of journey into a small shelf.
st: Invent a trip with three needs: finding your way, understanding a place and enjoying a quiet hour.
Browse ordinary shelves or the public catalogue for one title that could serve each need. Three different subjects are welcome; you need not read or borrow the books.
Record each title and its job. Choose which one you would take if your imaginary bag held only one, and explain what you would give up.
Leave books as the library requests and save your three-title packing list.

q.s: Let a few street words take an invented turn.
st: Collect five ordinary words visible in public-facing shopfronts, menus or street signs. Use individual words rather than slogans, brand names or private messages.
Choose three of them and write a two-sentence invented story about something arriving by water. The story can be playful or quiet.
Replace one chosen word with another from your list. Notice how the second version changes the scene.
Save both versions and mark your favourite line. If reading the surroundings is difficult, use river, door, light, shade and home instead.
